lead: A spark plug carries the coil's high voltage into the combustion chamber, seals the chamber, and fires a spark across a small gap shortly before top dead centre on the compression stroke. The voltage needed to break the gap is not fixed: it rises with gap size and cylinder pressure, and falls when the electrodes are hot. The coil must offer more voltage than the plug needs, with enough stored energy to keep the spark alive. If it cannot, the engine misfires, first under full load. This chapter covers plug construction, heat range, the firing voltage and the path the high-voltage pulse takes.
prereq: You need: the coil, dwell and stored energy from ignition fundamentals.

blocks.text: The plug is a steel shell around a ceramic insulator. A terminal at the top takes the high-tension cable. The insulator is alumina ceramic; it holds the centre electrode and carries heat from the tip to the shell. The centre electrode tip faces one or more earth electrodes welded to the shell. The shell screws into the cylinder head and gives the earth return. In a resistor plug a resistor of a few kilohms, set in a conductive glass seal below the terminal, cuts radio-frequency noise; the glass seal also stops combustion gas leaking up the centre. A copper core in the centre electrode carries heat away, and platinum or iridium tips resist erosion.

Heat range is the plug's ability to shed heat from its tip to the shell. It is set mainly by the length of the insulator nose. A hot plug has a long nose: heat has a long path, so the tip runs hotter and burns off carbon and oil. It suits a lightly loaded engine whose plug would otherwise stay below the self-cleaning temperature, about 450 °C. A cold plug has a short nose: the tip runs cooler, so it does not glow and cause pre-ignition in a hot, high-power engine. Makers number heat ranges in opposite directions, so always fit the plug the engine maker lists.

The gap is the shortest distance between the centre and earth electrodes, set to about 0.7–1.1 mm. Too small a gap gives a short, weak spark that may not light the mixture; too large a gap raises the firing voltage beyond what the coil can give. Carbon or oil fouling builds a conducting layer on the insulator nose. That layer leaks the coil's energy to earth before the voltage can rise high enough to break the gap.

sections.h3: Firing voltage and the high-voltage circuit

blocks.text: The gas in the gap is an insulator until free electrons gain enough energy to ionise it. The voltage at which this avalanche starts is the firing voltage Vf. It rises when the gap is wider, because the field is weaker for the same voltage. It rises with cylinder pressure, because denser gas means the electrons collide before they gain enough energy. It falls when the electrodes are hot, because a hot surface releases electrons more easily, and it is higher with worn, rounded electrodes. Typical values are 10–20 kV at part load and up to 30–35 kV at full load on a high-compression or turbocharged engine.

blocks.where: V<sub>f</sub> is the firing voltage in kV and g the gap in mm. At light load the same engine needs only V<sub>f</sub> ≈ 5 + 12 g. These lines are for this example engine; every engine has its own.

blocks.text: The coil's available voltage is what it can deliver into an open circuit. At the break the primary emf rises to a few hundred volts (not 12 V), and the secondary gives roughly V₂ = n V₁, where n = N₂/N₁ is the turns ratio and V₁ the primary emf. A 1:100 coil with V₁ = 250 V gives 25 kV. The difference between available and required voltage is the voltage reserve; the engine runs only while the reserve is positive.

The high-voltage path is coil secondary → king lead → distributor cap centre → rotor → rotor gap → cap segment → plug lead → terminal → centre electrode → gap → earth electrode → shell → cylinder head → back to the coil through the engine earth. Each part adds loss: the rotor gap, lead resistance, a suppressor, and dirt or moisture tracking on the cap. The plug therefore sees less than the coil's ideal V₂.

sections.h3: The spark pulse: firing line, spark line, ringing

blocks.text: An oscilloscope on the secondary shows three stages after each break, and a service technician reads them. First the voltage shoots up the firing line until the gap breaks down, in a few microseconds. Then it drops to a low, roughly flat spark line of 1–2 kV while the arc burns for about 1–2 ms, using the stored energy. When the energy can no longer hold the arc, the spark goes out and the coil rings down in a few damped oscillations. A high firing line means a wide gap or an open lead; a short spark line means too little energy or a lean mixture.

blocks.where: E is the energy stored in the coil in joules (J), L the primary inductance in henries (H) and I the primary current at the break in amperes (A).

blocks.text: Too little energy gives a short spark that cannot light a lean or turbulent mixture; too much erodes the electrodes. A fouled or worn plug fires at idle and fails at full load: the cylinder pressure, and so Vf, rises with load, and the reserve runs out. The ECU of electronic and programmed ignition sets the dwell so the coil reaches its current at every speed.

examples.question: An electronic-ignition coil has primary inductance 8 mH and the primary current reaches 6 A at the break. Its turns ratio is 1:100 and the primary emf at the break is 250 V. (a) Find the energy stored. (b) Find the ideal secondary voltage. (c) Using the full-load line V<sub>f</sub> = 10 + 22 g, decide whether it fires a 0.9 mm gap at full load. (d) Find the largest gap it can fire at full load.
steps: L = 8 mH = 0.008 H and I = 6 A.
Reserve = 25 − 29.8 = −4.8 kV. The reserve is negative, so this plug misfires at full load (at light load it needs only 5 + 12 × 0.9 = 15.8 kV and fires).
Largest gap: 25 = 10 + 22 g, so g = 15 ÷ 22 = 0.68 mm.
examples.answer: (a) 144 mJ. (b) 25 kV. (c) The 0.9 mm gap needs 29.8 kV, 4.8 kV more than the coil gives, so it misfires at full load. (d) A gap of 0.68 mm or less fires.

traps: Multiplying the turns ratio by 12 V. The secondary voltage is n times the primary emf at the break, a few hundred volts.
Saying hot electrodes need more voltage. A hot surface frees electrons more easily, so the firing voltage falls; pressure and gap raise it.
A hot plug is not a plug for a hot engine. A hot plug suits a cool-running, lightly loaded engine; a cold plug suits a hot, high-power engine.
Mixing available voltage (what the coil can give) with required voltage (what the plug needs). The engine runs on the difference, the reserve.
Resistor plugs and suppressors cut radio noise; they add resistance in the secondary, not spark energy.

quiz.q: Define the heat range of a spark plug.
quiz.a: Heat range is the plug's ability to shed heat from its tip to the shell and cylinder head, set mainly by the length of the insulator nose.

quiz.q: Why does a hot plug suit a cool-running engine?
quiz.a: A lightly loaded engine keeps the plug tip cool. A hot plug, with its long insulator nose, holds more heat, so its tip reaches the self-cleaning temperature and burns off carbon and oil.

quiz.q: A coil has turns ratio 1:80 and a primary emf at the break of 300 V. Find the ideal secondary voltage in kV.
Use the full-load line V<sub>f</sub> = 10 + 22 g to find the voltage a 1.1 mm gap needs, and the reserve of a 30 kV coil.
quiz.a: V<sub>f</sub> = 10 + 22 × 1.1 = 10 + 24.2 = 34.2 kV. Reserve = 30 − 34.2 = −4.2 kV, so the plug misfires at full load; the gap must be closed up.

quiz.q: Why can a worn plug fire at idle but miss at full load?
quiz.a: Full load raises the cylinder pressure, so the firing voltage rises; wear widens and rounds the gap, which raises it further. The coil's available voltage is fixed, so the reserve that was positive at idle becomes negative under load and no spark forms.

quiz.q: Name two secondary losses in a distributor ignition system and state their effect.
quiz.a: The rotor gap and the lead or suppressor resistance (also dirt tracking on the cap). Each takes part of the coil's voltage or leaks charge before it reaches the plug, so less voltage is available at the gap.

quiz.q: What do the firing line and the spark line on a secondary oscilloscope trace show?
quiz.a: The firing line is the voltage needed to break down the gap, about 10–20 kV. The spark line is the lower voltage, 1–2 kV, that holds the arc for about 1–2 ms while the stored energy lasts.

beyond: Iridium and platinum fine-wire plugs keep their gap for 100 000 km or more, and coil-on-plug removes the distributor losses altogether. Lean-burn and high-boost engines need very high firing voltages, so research looks at multiple sparks, longer spark lines and corona ignition. Search terms: spark plug heat range, firing voltage, voltage reserve, ignition oscilloscope patterns, corona ignition.
